title: Inside Kerala's Spiral Coffee House: Laurie Baker's Architectural Gem That Looks Like a Giant Cake
excerpt: The Indian Coffee House in Thiruvananthapuram, designed by British-born architect Laurie Baker, draws visitors with its spiraling brick ramp, no-window design, and affordable South Indian fare.
body:
• The Indian Coffee House in Thiruvananthapuram is a spiraling cylindrical building designed by British-born architect Laurie Baker, often called the "Gandhi of Indian architecture"
  • The building uses no windows — instead, Baker's signature brick jaali walls provide natural ventilation and light, eliminating the need for fans or air conditioning
  • A continuous spiral ramp takes diners from ground floor to the top, with built-in stone tables and benches along the outer edge, saving the cost of furniture
  • The worker-owned cooperative serves South Indian staples like masala dosa, appam, and filter coffee at prices that rarely exceed a few hundred rupees

A Building That Defies Convention

Across from Thiruvananthapuram's central railway station, a cylindrical brick-red structure rises in tiers, looking less like a restaurant and more like a giant cake — or perhaps a lighthouse that wandered inland. This is the Indian Coffee House, one of Kerala's most recognizable buildings and a masterwork of the architect who designed over 1,000 structures across India while keeping most of them affordable enough for ordinary people.

Designed by Lawrence Wilfred Baker — the British-born, Padma Shri-winning architect better known as Laurie Baker — the building was commissioned by the Coffee Board, most likely constructed around 1980 to 1990. The brief was deceptively simple: design a cost-effective restaurant on a small plot of land that could potentially be replicated in other cities.

Baker's solution was anything but ordinary.

"He had developed a distinct architectural language that was vernacular yet modern, and the Indian Coffee House in Trivandrum is a great example of that."

— Jaigopal Rao, Co-founder and Head of Designs, Inspiration Collective, Kochi

The Spiral That Replaces Stairs

Walk through the entrance and the building's genius reveals itself immediately. There are no stairs. Instead, a continuous circular ramp winds upward from the ground floor to the top, much like a parking garage — except that along one side of the ramp sit tables and benches cast directly into stone. On the other side is the walkway.

The building is wider at the base and tapers toward the top to maintain structural balance. The outer wall is constructed entirely of Baker's trademark brick jaali — a perforated screen that lets fresh air and diffused light flow through the interior without any windows. There are no fans. No air conditioning. In a city where daytime temperatures regularly cross 30°C, the building stays comfortable through design alone.

According to architect Jaigopal Rao, as described in Paper Planes, the Indian Coffee House was originally conceived as a self-service establishment. The ground floor had a billing counter where diners could collect a coupon, pick up their food, and walk up the ramp — sitting at lower tables if they were in a rush, or continuing to the top for a leisurely meal. While self-service never took off and white-uniformed waiters became an integral part of the experience, the design proves its timelessness by functioning as smoothly today as it did decades ago.

Baker's Philosophy in Brick

Baker, who moved to Kerala in the late 1960s after working in the Himalayan region, spent most of his professional life in Thiruvananthapuram. He built for fishermen, tribal communities, and low-income families. He rummaged through salvage heaps for building materials. He received India's Padma Shri in 1990 and the Indian Institute of Architects' Madhav Achwal Gold Medal, yet his greatest mark was on the hundreds of homes and public buildings he designed using local materials — brick, laterite, timber, and stone — at a fraction of what steel-and-concrete construction would cost.

The Coffee House embodies every Baker principle: curved walls that enclose more volume at lower material cost, locally sourced brick construction, climate-responsive design that eliminates energy consumption, and an aesthetic that is unmistakably modern yet rooted in Kerala's building traditions.

What to Eat and How to Get There

The Indian Coffee House chain is run as a workers' cooperative society — employees collectively own and manage the business. The first such society was formed in Bengaluru in 1957, and the chain now has over 400 outlets across India, though none match the architectural distinction of the Thiruvananthapuram branch.

The menu is South Indian comfort food at prices that make the upscale restaurants of nearby Gurugram look obscene: masala dosa with its distinctive beetroot tint, appam, poori masala, chicken cutlets, beef fry, and what regulars insist is some of the best filter coffee in Kerala. A full meal for two rarely exceeds a few hundred rupees.

Located in the Thampanoor area, right opposite the railway station and near the bus terminal, the Coffee House is impossible to miss — and for the thousands of Keralite NRIs who return home each year, it remains an essential stop, as much for nostalgia as for the dosa.
nri_angle: The Indian Coffee House is a nostalgic landmark for Keralite NRIs worldwide and sits steps from Thiruvananthapuram's central railway station, making it an essential stop for diaspora travelers visiting Kerala.
